name: Modus Ponens
pattern_description: From p → q and p, conclude q.
natural_language: The tautology (p ∧(p→q))→qis the basis of the rule of inference called modus ponens, or the law of detachment.
full_explanation: 1.6 Rules of Inference 75 validity of some relatively simple argument forms, called rules of inference. These rules of inference can be used as building blocks to construct more complicated valid argument forms. We will now introduce the most important rules of inference in propositional logic. The tautology (p ∧(p→q))→qis the basis of the rule of inference called modus ponens, or the law of detachment. (Modus ponens is Latin for mode that affirms.) This tautology leads to the following valid argument form, which we have already seen in our initial discussion aboutarguments (where, as before, the symbol ∴denotes “therefore”): pp→q ∴q Using this notation, the hypotheses are written in a column, followed by a horizontal bar, fol-lowed by a line that begins with the therefore symbol and ends with the conclusion. In particular,modus ponens tells us that if a conditional statement and the hypothesis of this conditional state-ment are both true, then the conclusion must also be true. Example 1 illustrates the use of modusponens. EXAMPLE 1 Suppose that the conditional statement “If it snows today, then we will go skiing” and its hy-pothesis, “It is snowing today,” are true. name: Implication Introduction
pattern_description: Assume p and derive q; then conclude p → q (conditional proof).
natural_language: To prove a conditional p → q, begin by assuming p and derive q; this establishes the implication.
full_explanation: Section 1.7 explains that a direct proof of a conditional statement p→q starts by assuming p is true and then, using axioms, definitions, previously proved theorems, and rules of inference, derives q. This prevents the only falsifying case (p true and q false), so p→q is established. This is the conditional-proof pattern used in implication introduction.

name: Negation Introduction
pattern_description: Assume p and derive a contradiction (⊥); then conclude ¬p (proof by contradiction).
natural_language: If assuming p leads to contradiction, p must be false; therefore ¬p.
full_explanation: Section 1.7 presents proof by contradiction as showing that an assumption leads to an impossibility. If assuming p yields a contradiction (such as r ∧ ¬r), the assumption cannot hold, so ¬p follows. Rosen uses this structure repeatedly when deriving a contradiction from an assumption and then rejecting that assumption.

name: Falsum Elimination
pattern_description: From contradiction (⊥), infer any formula (ex falso quodlibet).
natural_language: A contradiction marks an impossible state; once ⊥ is reached, any target statement is derivable in classical reasoning.
full_explanation: Section 1.7 formalizes contradiction via expressions like r ∧ ¬r and uses contradiction to force rejection of assumptions. In this framework, once a contradiction is obtained, the current assumption context is inconsistent, which licenses deriving any formula in classical logic (the ex falso principle), typically used as a subproof-closing step.
